article.title: Why Causal Inference Starts With the Counterfactual
article.why: 從 counterfactual 出發理解 randomization、confounding、quasi-experiments 與增量效果，避免把相關性當因果。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

paragraphs.en:
Causal inference begins with a question that can never be observed directly: what would have happened to the same unit, at the same time, if the treatment had not occurred? That unobserved alternative is the counterfactual. Most of the difficulty in causal analysis comes from constructing a credible substitute for it.

Suppose a company launches a retention campaign and the targeted customers renew at a rate of 72%. The number may look impressive, but it does not tell us the campaign's causal effect. Those customers might have renewed at 70% without any message, in which case the incremental effect is small. Or they might have renewed at only 50%, in which case the campaign is highly valuable. The observed outcome after treatment is only half of the causal comparison.

A common mistake is to compare treated customers with untreated customers without asking why the two groups differ. If marketers target people who appear most likely to renew, the treated group may outperform even when the campaign does nothing. If they target customers at high risk of leaving, the treated group may underperform even when the campaign helps substantially. Selection into treatment creates a confounding problem because treatment status is related to factors that also affect the outcome.

Randomized experiments solve this problem elegantly when they are feasible. Random assignment makes treatment independent, on average, of both observed and unobserved pre-treatment characteristics. The control group then becomes a credible estimate of the treated group's counterfactual. The causal effect is estimated by comparing outcomes across the randomized groups, subject to issues such as noncompliance, attrition, interference, and sampling variation.

But many important decisions cannot be randomized. Governments cannot randomly assign recessions. Companies may not be able to randomize a major pricing change across customers for legal or commercial reasons. A new regulation may apply to one region and not another. In these settings, analysts use observational designs that try to recreate the logic of a counterfactual.

Difference-in-differences is one example. Instead of comparing two groups only after a policy change, the method compares how their outcomes changed over time. If the treated region improved by ten points while a comparable untreated region improved by four, the additional six-point change may be attributed to the policy under assumptions such as parallel trends. The design is stronger than a simple before-and-after comparison because it subtracts changes that affected both groups, but its credibility depends on whether the comparison group really provides a useful counterfactual trend.

Regression discontinuity uses a different source of quasi-randomness. If treatment is assigned by a threshold, such as a score of 70 or higher, units just above and just below the cutoff may be very similar except for treatment status. Near the threshold, the comparison can approximate an experiment. However, the estimated effect is usually local: it applies most clearly to units near the cutoff, not necessarily to everyone.

Instrumental variables provide another strategy when an external factor changes the probability of treatment without directly changing the outcome except through that treatment. This requirement is powerful but demanding. A variable that merely predicts treatment is not automatically a valid instrument. Analysts need a substantive argument for why the exclusion restriction is plausible.

Matching and regression adjustment are often useful, but they do not remove every source of bias. They can balance observed characteristics, not variables that were never measured or measured badly. A model with many controls can still produce a biased causal estimate if an important confounder remains hidden. Statistical sophistication does not replace design logic.

The counterfactual perspective also changes how businesses think about KPIs. Suppose customers who receive a sales call spend more afterward than customers who do not. A predictive interpretation asks, “Who spends more?” A causal interpretation asks, “For whom does the call increase spending compared with what that same person would otherwise have spent?” The people with the highest expected spending are not always the people with the highest treatment effect.

This distinction matters for targeting. A company can waste resources by contacting customers who were going to buy anyway. In uplift modeling or heterogeneous treatment-effect analysis, the goal is not simply to rank customers by outcome probability. It is to estimate differences between potential outcomes under alternative actions. That makes the target the incremental response rather than the raw response.

Good causal work therefore starts before the model. Analysts should define the treatment, outcome, population, timing, and causal estimand. They should draw or at least reason through the pathways that could create confounding, measurement bias, or interference. They should ask what event or comparison makes the counterfactual believable. Only then should they choose an estimation method.

Sensitivity analysis is equally important. Because causal claims rest on assumptions, analysts should test how conclusions change when those assumptions are weakened. In observational work, a precise estimate can still be unconvincing if a small amount of hidden bias would reverse it. Conversely, a somewhat noisy estimate from a strong design may be more decision-useful than a highly precise association from a weak design.

The deepest lesson is that causality is not a property automatically produced by a regression coefficient, a machine-learning model, or a large dataset. It is a property of a comparison supported by assumptions and evidence. The counterfactual gives the comparison its meaning. Whenever someone says that a policy, campaign, product feature, or intervention “caused” an outcome, the first question should be: compared with what credible alternative?
paragraphs.zh: 因果效果的核心是無法同時觀察的 counterfactual：同一單位如果沒有接受 treatment 會怎樣。隨機實驗用 control group 近似這個反事實；觀察性研究則靠設計與假設建立可信替代。模型再複雜，也不能取代 counterfactual 的比較邏輯。
paragraphs.ja: 因果推論の中心には、同じ対象が処置を受けなかった場合にどうなっていたかという観測不能な反実仮想があります。ランダム化比較では対照群がその近似になります。観察研究では差の差、回帰不連続、操作変数などの設計と仮定によって反実仮想を構成します。高度なモデルだけでは因果性は生まれません。

vocabulary.usage: Causal inference asks about an unobserved counterfactual.
Treatment can be a campaign, policy, or product change.
Estimate the incremental effect of the campaign.
Selection into treatment can create confounding.
Regression discontinuity can exploit quasi-randomness near a cutoff.
A valid instrument must satisfy strong assumptions.
The exclusion restriction needs a substantive argument.
Define the causal estimand before modeling.
Use sensitivity analysis to test assumptions.

phrases.explanation: 反事實問題的典型形式
phrases.example: Ask what would have happened without the treatment.

phrases.explanation: 誰會進入處置組的選擇機制
phrases.example: Selection into treatment can bias a simple comparison.
The design relies on a plausible parallel-trends assumption.

phrases.explanation: 回歸不連續設計的局部區域
phrases.example: Units near the cutoff may be highly comparable.

phrases.explanation: 未觀測混雜造成的偏誤
phrases.example: Test how much hidden bias would change the conclusion.

grammar.title: what would have happened if ...
grammar.body: 過去反事實常用 would have + p.p. 與 if + past perfect，表達沒有發生但用來比較的情境。

grammar.title: subject to + noun
grammar.body: 正式分析語氣，表示結果成立但仍受某些限制，例如 subject to attrition and sampling variation。

grammar.title: not automatically
grammar.body: 用於切斷錯誤推論，例如 predictive power does not automatically imply causal validity。

grammar.title: under assumptions such as ...
grammar.body: 因果分析應明示識別所依賴的假設，而不是只報 estimator。

business.term: What is the counterfactual for this KPI movement?
business.explanation: 先問沒有介入時會怎樣
business.example: Before claiming impact, what is the counterfactual for this KPI movement?
How was treatment assigned, and could that assignment be related to the outcome?
What identifies the causal effect in this design?

business.term: Is the estimate local or generalizable?
business.example: The cutoff estimate is credible, but is it local or generalizable?

business.term: Which assumption would reverse the conclusion if violated?
business.example: Which assumption would reverse the conclusion if violated?

quiz.question: Why is a 72% renewal rate after a campaign not enough to estimate causal impact?
quiz.answer: Because we do not know what the same targeted customers would have done without the campaign.

quiz.question: What problem does random assignment address?
quiz.answer: It makes treatment independent, on average, of pre-treatment characteristics that affect outcomes.

quiz.question: Output: Turn a predictive question into a causal question.
quiz.answer: Example: Instead of 'Who will buy?', ask 'Whose probability of buying increases because of the message?'
